newsitem.title: UK: West can profit from Asian mistrust of Japan - Lee.
newsitem.headline: West can profit from Asian mistrust of Japan - Lee.

text.p: Western companies should not be deterred from investing in East Asia by a false belief that Japan will have a monopoly in markets there, Singapore's Senior Minister Lee Kuan Yew said on Tuesday.
In a speech to the Asia House economic and cultural forum in London, Lee said countries in the area wanted to balance their dependence on Japan by wooing the United States and Europe.

"This is because East Asia's history is one of intense rivalry and mistrust between Japan and China, Korea and the several Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) countries that suffered badly in World War Two," Lee said.
He pointed to recent rows over different groups of "disputed islands" between countries in the region as evidence of the tensions that existed.
On Monday, Taiwanese and Hong Kong protesters briefly broke through a Japanese cordon to land on disputed islands in the East China Sea, sparking a diplomatic row.

Sovereignty of the Spratly islands in the South China Sea, claimed in whole or part by China, Taiwan, the Philippines, Vietnam, Malaysia and Brunei, would remain a problem for many Asian countries, Lee said.
"Western companies can therefore capitalise on the diversities and insecurities in Asia."
Lee, Singapore's long-time prime minister and now senior minister in the office of current premier Goh Chok Tong, is on a trip to Britain and the United States.
He said firms would inevitably experience some frustration in the evolving economic and political conditions.

"In some of these countries, political systems are still weak. As a result, frequent changes in investment rules and regulations occur. Politicians, despite their good intentions of reform, may be voted out of power."
In some countries, there was no stable rule of law, "and property rights are new concepts in their laws", he added.
Singapore, highly familiar with market conditions in the area, could help companies reduce their risks, Lee said.
It could serve as a regional base or help foster strategic alliances to allow companies to invest in third countries.
And it could provide western companies with "a convenient foothold" in the industrial parks that are built and managed by Singapore in China, India, Indonesia and Vietnam, Lee said.
ASEAN comprises Brunei, Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, the Philippines, Thailand and Vietnam.
